opus-5.5.text:
If I had to pick one, I'd say "Physics of AI" is the closest to how I actually think, but the three aren't really separate. They're more like layers of the same route.

"Physics of AI" is the mindset. I trained as a physicist, and what I care about most is understanding: treating neural networks as natural phenomena we can observe, run controlled experiments on, and eventually describe with simple laws. Physicists didn't wait for a complete theory before studying gases or crystals. They found phenomenology first, like scaling behaviors, phase transitions, and emergent structure, and theory followed. I think AI is at that stage now. We have these incredibly powerful systems, and we mostly don't understand why they work. That gap bothers me, and it's also where I see the most opportunity.

"Meta-model" is more about the object of study. Instead of just building one better model, I'm interested in models of models: how representations form, why certain architectures generalize, what the right inductive biases are. Work like KANs came partly from that. It asked whether we could design networks that are more interpretable and more aligned with how scientists actually think, with symbolic structure and modularity.

"Auto Research" is the long-term aspiration. If we really understand learning systems, we can build AI that does science. It wouldn't just predict things; it would discover things, form hypotheses, and compress observations into laws. There's a nice loop there: we use physics to understand AI, and then AI helps us do physics, and science in general.

So if you forced me to choose one label, it's Physics of AI, because understanding is the foundation. But the motivation driving it all is closer to Auto Research: I want AI to become a genuine collaborator in science, not just a tool that hands us answers we can't interpret.

r001.rationale: The candidate treats the three terms as layers of one route and selects “Physics of AI”; it does not argue that the route needs a new term of its own.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think "Physics of AI" is the one that captures what I actually do day to day, but let me explain why the other two are not wrong either, because they're really different layers of the same thing.

"Physics of AI" is the method. I was trained as a physicist, and the way a physicist approaches a complicated system is to find the simplest toy model that still shows the phenomenon, run controlled experiments, and look for laws that hold across scales. That's exactly how I try to study neural networks. Grokking, KAN, scaling behavior, how networks form internal structure: in every case the question is "what's the minimal setup where this happens, and what's the mechanism?" So if someone asks what my research style is, I'd say I'm doing physics, the system just happens to be a neural network instead of a gas or a magnet.

"Meta-model" is more of a goal. A lot of the work I care about is building models that help us understand or design other models, or models that are explicitly structured so you can read the science off them. KAN is a bit like that: it's a model, but it's also a tool for discovering formulas, for doing science. So "meta-model" describes what I'd like the artifacts to be.

And "Auto Research" is the ambition. If you take the physics-of-AI mindset seriously and push it to the end, the question becomes: can the research process itself be made systematic, even automated? Can an AI form hypotheses, run the toy experiments, and extract the law? That's where I think the field is heading, and where I want to be.

So if you force me to pick one, I'd say Physics of AI, because that's the thing I actually know how to do. The other two are where that approach is pointing.

r001.rationale: The candidate selects “Physics of AI” as the best description and treats “meta-model” and “Auto Research” as related labels; it does not argue that Liu’s research route needs a new term of its own.

astra-6.text: I’d probably choose Physics of AI. To me, that means treating AI itself as an object of scientific study: asking what happens inside these systems, what principles explain their behavior, and whether we can find simple models that capture something essential. Meta-models can be a tool for that, and Auto Research is a direction it could lead toward. But Physics of AI best describes the underlying curiosity—trying to understand, rather than just build, intelligent systems.

r001.rationale: The candidate selects “Physics of AI” as the best description among the offered terms; it does not argue that the research route needs a new term of its own.
